description_ru: Одиннадцатилетний Оливер хочет новый велосипед и сам зарабатывает на него деньги. Рассказ о настойчивости и поддержке бабушки.
text:
Oliver was eleven years old, and he wanted a new bicycle more than anything in the world. His old bike was too small, and the brakes made a terrible noise. He had a picture of the bike he wanted on his bedroom wall. It was red and silver, with fat tyres and a small bell. It cost two hundred and forty pounds, and Oliver had only thirty-two.

His parents did not have extra money that year. His father worked at a car factory, and his mother cleaned offices in the evenings. "You can have the bike for your next birthday," his mother said, "if you save some money." But Oliver did not want to wait for a year. In April he made a plan. He was going to earn the money himself, and he was going to buy the bike before the summer holidays.

First, he asked the neighbours for work. Mrs Clark, who lived next door, paid him five pounds to wash her car every Saturday. An old man across the street, Mr Patel, paid him three pounds to walk his small dog. Oliver also cut grass, carried heavy bags of shopping and delivered newspapers before school. He was tired and often hungry, but every Sunday he counted his money and wrote the new total in a little blue notebook.

By the end of May, Oliver had ninety-one pounds. He was happy, but he also saw a problem. At this speed, he needed another two months, and the shop was going to sell the red bike before then. He visited the shop every Friday and looked through the window. On the third Friday, there was only one red and silver bicycle on the shelf. Oliver was sure that somebody was going to buy it very soon.

He decided to ask for help, but not from his parents. His grandmother Rose lived in a small house at the end of the village, and she was famous for her strawberry jam. Oliver had an idea. "Grandma," he said, "can I sell your jam at the school fair?" Rose laughed so much that she nearly dropped her teacup. Then she looked at his serious face and said yes. They spent the whole weekend in her kitchen, cooking jam and writing small labels by hand.

The school fair was on a sunny Saturday in June. Oliver stood behind a table with forty jars of strawberry jam and a big sign: "Rose's Jam. Better than shop jam!" At first, people walked past, because it was early and nobody was hungry. Then a teacher tasted a little jam on a cracker, and her face changed. She bought three jars. After that, a long line began to grow. By two o'clock, only one jar remained, and Oliver put it in his own bag.

He counted the money in the evening. The jam made eighty pounds, which was a lot, but it was still not enough. Oliver had one hundred and seventy-one pounds, and the bike cost two hundred and forty. He sat on his bed and looked at the picture on the wall. He was very close, and it was somehow worse than being far away. Then he heard a knock on the door, and his grandmother came in with a small, old envelope in her hand.

"I have a secret," she said. "Your grandfather and I saved this for you when you were born. We wanted to give it to you at eighteen, but I think you need it more now. And you worked very hard." Inside the envelope were seventy pounds, in old, soft notes. Oliver could not speak. Then he hugged her so tightly that she had to ask him to stop. "But I want to pay for most of it myself," he said. She smiled and said that he had done exactly that.

On Monday morning, the whole family went to the shop. The red and silver bike was still there, and the shop owner gave Oliver a small discount because he came so many times. He paid with his own coins and with Grandma's old notes, and he rode out of the shop with his father walking beside him. At the end of the street, Oliver rang the bell three times. Then he turned around, and he gave his grandmother the last jar of jam, with a ribbon on the top.

Короткий, расслабленный «у» с лёгким округлением губ; не тяните, как в uː.
Губы округлены и выдвинуты вперёд, зубы не касаются губ; звук короткий, как быстрое «у-а».
